questions.q: Name the five supporting characters in "Glory at Twilight" who directly interact with Satyajit during the wedding events at Shantipur.
questions.a: Uncle Srinath, the village schoolmaster, Harish the moneylender, Beena (the bride), and the groom's father. A wrong answer that includes Satyajit's wife or the forgerer shows the student cannot distinguish between characters physically present in the wedding scenes and those only remembered or mentioned.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Uncle Srinath calls his daughters' marriages a "daughter crisis" and what this phrase reveals about his attitude toward Satyajit.
questions.a: Srinath views his daughters' weddings as recurring financial emergencies ("crisis") that he expects Satyajit to solve, revealing he sees Satyajit primarily as a financial resource rather than a relative. A wrong answer focusing only on the literal meaning of "crisis" misses the transactional nature of their relationship and Srinath's exploitation of Satyajit's past generosity.

questions.q: Using the four-column method (appearance, dialogue about Satyajit, desire, Satyajit's reaction), analyze the village schoolmaster's character in the scene where he addresses the gathering.
questions.a: Appearance: old, coughing, superior glance. Dialogue: claims he always knew Satyajit had "light of genius," predicted High Court judgeship, mentions "perpetual feud" with young Satyajit. Desire: public validation of his past judgment, social status through association with success. Satyajit's reaction: laughs at the absurd prediction, feels "twinge of regret" for not visiting earlier. A wrong answer that omits the schoolmaster's self-serving motive fails to see how he mirrors the village's opportunistic homage.

questions.q: Compare and contrast how Harish the moneylender and Uncle Srinath evaluate Satyajit's worth. What does this comparison reveal about the story's view of social capital versus financial reality?
questions.a: Srinath values Satyajit's perceived status ("millionaire's word") as social capital for village prestige; Harish values only tangible collateral (house and pond) because he operates on financial reality. The contrast exposes the fragility of reputation-based honour in a cash economy. A wrong answer that treats both as merely "greedy" misses the structural commentary on how colonial-era feudal homage clashes with modern credit systems.

questions.q: Evaluate the narrative decision to keep Beena largely silent during the foot-washing scene. Does her silence make her a passive victim or a dignified participant? Justify with textual evidence.
questions.a: Beena's silence combined with "keen care" in washing feet and "shy, slender with large pensive eyes" portrays dignified participation in ritual, not victimhood. She performs her prescribed role gracefully, contrasting with the women's frantic fanning and Srinath's boasting. A wrong answer calling her "oppressed" imposes modern feminist reading without acknowledging the text's presentation of her agency within tradition.

questions.q: Write a 50-word inner monologue for the forgerer (from Satyajit's flashback) speaking to Satyajit on the train, using the phrase "wheel of fortune" to connect their fates.
questions.a: "You turned my trembling hand into your ladder, Satyajit. My wife's TB became your first rung. Now your wheel has spun full circle — my shame feeds your pride, your ruin feeds my peace. We are both crushed by the same wheel; difference is, I knew I was falling." A poor answer would lack the ironic reversal or misuse "wheel of fortune" as mere decoration.
